opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most exciting directions we have. The basic idea is pretty simple: alignment research is a kind of intellectual work, and if our models keep getting more capable, at some point they should be able to do a lot of that work for us, or at least with us. So rather than trying to solve the whole alignment problem for arbitrarily superintelligent systems right now, which is really hard because we don't even know what those systems will look like, we can set ourselves a more modest goal: align a system that's roughly human-level at alignment research, and then use that system to help us make progress on the harder problems.

One way I think about it is that there's an asymmetry between evaluation and generation. For a lot of tasks, it's much easier to check whether an answer is good than to come up with the answer yourself. If you ask a model to propose an alignment technique or write a proof or find a flaw in some code, it can be really valuable even if we couldn't have produced it, as long as we can evaluate it. And then we can use models to help with the evaluation too. That's the core of scalable oversight: AI assisting humans in supervising other AI.

With each successive generation of GPT models, you can already see this starting to happen in small ways. The models are useful for writing code, summarizing papers, critiquing outputs, generating test cases, and finding bugs. Those are all pieces of the research workflow. The hope is that as we go from one generation to the next, the fraction of the work the models can meaningfully contribute keeps growing. Each generation can help us align and oversee the next one a bit better.

Now, I want to be clear that this isn't a free lunch. There are real risks. If you're relying on a system to help with alignment research, you need to trust it enough that it isn't subtly steering you wrong. So a big part of the work is building the tools to validate that trust: interpretability, adversarial testing, deliberately training deceptive models to see if our techniques catch them, and so on. You also want the models you rely on to be no more capable than necessary for the task, because the more narrow and less agentic they are, the less you have to worry about.

But overall, I'm fairly optimistic. I think alignment research might actually be one of the easier things to automate in the sense that it needs less dangerous capability than, say, building new technologies in the physical world. And if we can get these models to substantially accelerate alignment research, we have a much better shot at keeping up with capabilities progress than if humans had to do it all on their own.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes current and hoped-for ways GPT models could contribute, but does not advocate empirically testing whether successive generations can usefully assist alignment research.

r002.rationale: The candidate supports using capable models for alignment research, but does not call for being ready to pursue that work intensively as soon as the models become useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really at the heart of how I think about the whole alignment problem. The basic idea is that alignment research is itself a kind of cognitive labor, and if we're building systems that are increasingly good at cognitive labor, we should be using them to help us do that research.

So the way I'd frame it is: we don't need to solve the entire alignment problem ourselves, right now, with human researchers alone. What we need to do is figure out how to align a system that's roughly as capable as a good human alignment researcher, and then use that system to accelerate the work. And then as the next generation comes along, you use the previous one, plus the tools and techniques you've developed, to align that one, and so on. It's a bootstrapping process.

What I find compelling about this is that each step is much smaller than the whole problem. If you ask, "how do we align a superintelligence?" that's a really daunting question and I don't think anyone has a good answer today. But if you ask, "how do we align a model that's slightly better than GPT-4 at writing code and running experiments and critiquing papers?" that feels much more tractable. We have a lot of levers for that: RLHF, scalable oversight techniques like critiques and debate, interpretability tools that let us look inside the model.

Now, there are some important caveats. The first is that you have to actually trust the system you're delegating to. If you hand off alignment research to a model that's subtly misaligned, it might produce research that looks great but has a flaw baked in, and you might not catch it. So a big part of the research agenda is building the evaluation and oversight tools that let you verify what the model gives you, rather than just taking its word for it. You want to be in a regime where checking the work is easier than doing the work, and I think that's often true for research.

The second caveat is that you want the capability curve and the alignment curve to be moving together. If models get much more capable before we've figured out how to use them for alignment, you lose the window where the model is capable enough to help but not so capable that you can't oversee it. So there's some urgency to actually trying this now, with the models we have, even though they're not that good at it yet. Right now GPT-4 can do bits and pieces: it can help with literature review, write some code, find bugs in experiments. It's not going to independently come up with a new alignment agenda. But the hope is that we learn what it takes to make these systems useful for this kind of work, and that lesson compounds.

And honestly, I think this is just what's going to happen regardless. Every field is going to get transformed by these models doing more and more of the intellectual work. The question is whether alignment research gets the benefit of that as early and as deliberately as possible, so we're not playing catch-up.

r001.rationale: The response urges trying model-assisted alignment research now and describes using each generation to help align the next, learning what makes the models useful as capabilities improve.

r002.rationale: It stresses urgency, says to start with current models despite their limits, and describes using more capable successive models to accelerate alignment research as soon as they can help.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that we should try to use the capabilities of these models to help us solve alignment. As models get more capable, they should become more useful research assistants: they can help write code, think through experiments, critique proposals, and eventually help us understand where our alignment techniques are failing.

You can imagine doing this iteratively. You align a model well enough that you can trust it to help you with some parts of alignment research, and then you use that help to develop better techniques for the next generation. That next generation can then help you tackle harder problems.

Of course, a lot is hidden in “well enough.” We need to be able to evaluate the work the model does. If it produces an alignment proposal that sounds very convincing, but we can’t tell whether it actually works, that doesn’t solve the problem. So I’d want to start with tasks where we can check the results, like implementing experiments or finding problems in code, and expand from there as we get better at oversight.

The hope is that we don’t have to solve the entire problem unaided. We can get increasingly capable systems to help us, while maintaining our ability to understand and check the important steps. But whether that process keeps working as the systems become much smarter is a central research question.

r001.rationale: It proposes using successive generations to help with alignment research and starting with checkable tasks, which communicates empirically testing their usefulness.

r002.rationale: It describes iterative use as models become more capable, but does not clearly advocate being ready to pursue model-assisted research intensively as soon as they become useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic idea is that we should use the models we have today to help us figure out how to align the next generation of models. And then, as those models become more capable, we can use them to help with the next step after that.

You don’t need a model that can solve the whole alignment problem for this to be useful. It could help you write code for experiments, critique a proposed approach, or find cases where another model behaves in ways you didn’t intend. Those are all pieces of alignment research that we can start handing over gradually.

The central difficulty is evaluation. If a model proposes an alignment technique, how do we know that it actually works? We can’t just ask the same model whether it did a good job and take its word for it. We need experiments and checks that give us evidence we can trust, even as more of the work is being done by AI.

So I’d like to build this up incrementally: start with tasks where we can evaluate the output quite reliably, learn how to supervise models doing that work, and then expand the scope. The hope is that we can get a lot of useful assistance with alignment before we have systems whose capabilities substantially exceed our ability to oversee them.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using current models to help align later generations and recommends starting with reliably evaluated tasks, using experiments and checks to assess the work.

r002.rationale: It recommends gradually expanding model assistance, but does not say to be ready to pursue it intensively as soon as models become capable enough.
